question.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-sin\,(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
